thesis: Generate IDs locally from time plus node identity plus randomness or a sequence, so no request waits on a central counter. Choose the format for the properties you need: sortability, index locality, size, and how much clock skew you can tolerate.
pitch: A central counter is a single point of failure and a cross-region round trip on every insert. Instead, each node generates IDs locally. The common choices are Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp, worker id, per-millisecond sequence), which are compact and time-ordered but need unique worker ids and care with clock skew; ULID or UUIDv7, 128 bits with a timestamp prefix plus randomness, which need no coordination and are roughly time-ordered, so they index well; and random UUIDv4, which needs no coordination but scatters inserts across a B-tree. For most systems today I'd pick UUIDv7: no worker-id management, good index locality, and a standard. I'd choose Snowflake-style when 64 bits matter for storage or a downstream system requires integers.

points.d: Every insert pays a network round trip, and the counter's availability caps the whole system's. Across regions that's tens of milliseconds per id and a cross-region dependency.

Timestamp in milliseconds, a worker id, and a sequence number per millisecond. Compact and sortable. Requires assigning unique worker ids (config, a lease in a coordination service) and handling clocks moving backwards.
48-bit millisecond timestamp prefix followed by random bits. No coordination, roughly time-ordered, standard 128-bit format (UUIDv7 is specified in RFC 9562).
Random UUIDv4 keys insert all over a B-tree, causing page splits and poor cache use at scale. Time-prefixed ids append near the right edge of the index.
Time-based ids assume clocks roughly agree. If a clock jumps back, a Snowflake generator must wait or refuse; UUIDv7 implementations typically keep a monotonic counter within a millisecond.
Time-ordered ids reveal creation time and, with sequences, volume. For public identifiers that matters; use an opaque external id if needed.

decision: Default: UUIDv7. Snowflake-style when you need 64-bit integers or strict per-node ordering and can manage worker ids. UUIDv4 when ordering is irrelevant and volume is low. Never a global counter on the hot path.
numbers: Snowflake capacity: with a 12-bit sequence, one worker can mint 4,096 ids per millisecond, about 4 million per second.
UUIDv7 has 74 bits of randomness and version info beyond the 48-bit timestamp; collision risk within one millisecond is negligible at realistic rates.
pitfalls: Reusing a worker id after a node is replaced, producing duplicates within the same millisecond.
Assuming time-ordered ids give a global order of events across regions; skew makes them only roughly ordered.
UUIDv4 primary keys on a very large, write-heavy table, then wondering why insert performance degrades.
Exposing sequential ids publicly, making enumeration and volume estimation trivial.

followups.q: How do you assign Snowflake worker ids safely?
followups.a: Lease them from a coordination service with a TTL, or derive them from stable infrastructure identity, and refuse to start if the lease can't be acquired.

followups.q: Can you sort events across regions by these ids?
followups.a: Only approximately. If you need a true order, use a single sequencer per partition or a logical clock; physical time can't give a total order under skew.

followups.q: What if the database wants integer keys?
followups.a: Snowflake-style 64-bit ids fit a bigint, or keep an internal bigint surrogate and expose a UUID externally.

example: A multi-region order system switches from a central sequence service to UUIDv7 generated in each service. Insert latency drops by the cross-region round trip, the sequence service disappears as a dependency, and index locality stays good because ids are time-prefixed.
